Even after Imperial authority collapsed, the Afar continued their service, refusing to completely succumb to the rising Geledi and instead crafting a witty deal of vassalage, which allowed them to retain almost complete autonomy under the protection of the Somalis.\nThey awaited patiently for the Civil War to end and for Ethiopia to return, and it seems like their wait is over. Immediately after receiving news of war, they kicked out the Somali overseers and turned to us, asking to rejoin the Empire and serve just like they did before.

When Somalia languished under Habesha rule, the Afar, our so-called 'brothers', chose to betray all those fighting to throw off the yoke and give up every last bit of their sovereignty, completely submitting to the oppressor. They adopted the Christian faith and fought relentlessly for the Empire upon the collapse of which we prayed. And after our prayers born fruit, they still refused to see the errors of their ways - they formed their own kingdom to save themselves from the devastation suffered by Habesha, and made a deal with us to come under our 'protection'.\nNow that the resurgent enemy is on our doorstep, we know how truly foolish we were to not annihilate them when we had the opportunity, as it became evident that we failed to convince them to do what is right. Upon hearing the news of Ethiopian armies crossing the border, they threw out all of our overseers and joined the enemy, betraying our cause and giving Ethiopia even more of an advantage.

Ethiopian troops have crossed the border, laying siege to several of our border fortresses. We have been waiting for this to happen for quite some time, and now we will finally destroy their petty state!

Why is this happening?
What did we do wrong?
It didn't have to be like that. Somalians, a bunch of tribesmen... Against a professional army? What can their horses do against artillery?
A lot, apparently.
Ethiopia is lost. Our core lands were spared, but the leadership wasn't. There is no regency anymore, no Emperor. There wasn't a peace agreement of any sort, they just occupied what they wanted and left what they didn't want. Is this really how the Empire meets its end?

With both the Emperor and many nobles dead, Ethiopia enters an interregnum. There was no central authority for a while, then an upstart was crowned a new Emperor. There were several upstarts, actually. Some of them were killed right away by angry mobs, some lost their first battle. Few made it to challenge the whole of Ethiopia. Just as we thought the Age of Princes was over, here came another one.

People die all the time. Of famine, of plague, of war. In the modern age, everyone blames violence of some sorts. Out of the aformentioned three, that would be war. But what if its negatives are exaggerated? Its death tolls overestimated?\nHow many lives did the original Age of Princes take? Nobody knows. But death was spread out over time. It was many people dying over years. And what about the Second Age of Princes? Many people died, we know that with much more certainty. Way more than died in the past, on average. Armies were bigger, methods were more brutal and effective. But it was quick, wasn't it? Not more than a few years. Maybe, it's better if many people die all at once, than over a large amount of time. Really, maybe more death brings peace faster?

Kassa Hailu in a big palace. Again. There were servants all around, but it was also eerily calm. At least, to Kassa. It didn't matter to him how it actually was. He had been in this environment for so long that it felt to him as if he already molded into it, became a part of the greater picture. Like a statue.
His familiarity with the usual flow of things also meant that he quickly noticed if there was something awry. And today was no simple day. Servants rushed across the palace, out of the window could be seen nobles and Marye's subordinates running around like ants on a disturbed anthill. It was never like that before!
Finally, a messenger arrived to Kassa Hailu. After the usual ceremonial, he finally broke the news.
'The Enderase is dead! He was shot dead in an ambush during a routine military campaign!'
The eerie calm returned. Followed by a ring in the ears. And a loud, almost deafening heartbeat.

Fot most of history, Ethiopia viewed the western tribes of the Nile as nothing more than a source of free workforce and soldiers with extremely twisted morals. During the Empire's height, we established tributary relations with the closest of these tribes, even converting some to Christianity. But full integration was never a consideration. Many factors push us to reevaluate this choice, but it is clearly too early to push for something this big. We will limit ourselves to seizing the borderlands, which are the most familiar with our ways, and prepare an expedition further west.

Violence is the most effective means to gain and control power, especially so in post-Zemene Mesafint Ethiopia. Being able to get hold of these means became the most important skills a polititian could have mastered. All sorts of methods were employed: bribes, flattery, clever reassignments and promotions, etc.\nThe two main sources of political power in Ethiopia made sure to do all of these things. However, in a state of diarchy, legitimacy, not legality, becomes the capital that makes people follow the orders. The Regency knew that it was on the backfoot there, as there is no way to legitimately justify keeping the Emperor in chains. And when He is an ambitious fellow, it becomes only a matter of time until he lures enough men to his side to upturn the existing order.\nThe Regency wasn't surprised when news came of several high-ranking military officers declaring allegiance directly to the Tewodros II and stopping all communication with the Regency. The Regency knew its time was running out: the Emperor now has the upper hand.

For quite some times, the town of Azezo, located a little south from Gonder, was calmer than usual. Suspiciously calmer. This didn't raise any alarms in the Regency, despite the fact that the town was a massive military camp from which the Regency operated. Previously, the magnitude of the bureaucratic bustle in the town was truly a sight to behold, as both military and civilian reports were coming in droves, to be analysed and acted on by the authorities. Of those, a significant amount held massive political importance, but these were becoming rarer and rarer. Until they stopped coming in entirely.\nThis was not a sign of things improving in the countryside, or the country's politics becoming a little easier to navigate. What the Regency didn't know was that Azezo was being slowly encircled by regiments that were formally loyal, but failed to report own movements. The calm was broken when an official tried to leave the town to visit their family - eyebrows were raised, then realisation came, and the alarms were sounded. But the assault was already underway. It was too late.

Political maneuvering is never an easy task, too dangerous for many. But, seemingly, not for Tewodros II - his incredibly successful endeavours in swaying the Ethiopian society, both the higher-ups and the smallfolk, have completely isolated the Regency. They have lost practically all influence, with all of their efforts to maintain some sort of relevance falling in vain. Now, the last remnants of them are trying to save their faces by defecting to the Emperor's side, while others flee across the border. They are not pursued - there is nothing to gain from catching these traitors.

Ethiopian retreat from Nubia was comparatively orderly and very much non-chaotic, something which cannot be said about the events that unfolded in Syria, Egypt and pretty much every other part of the Empire. The local administration already consisted majorly of Nubians, and dealings with them were as effective as it got in the Imperial bureaucracy due to the region's high levels of integration.\nThe new Kingdom that arose after our retreat was not so keen on rejoining the Empire, though. We have changed their minds by force, and with the reintegration of Nubia come all of the benefits of the lands, including a loyal population and vast amounts of resources.

There are many things one could say about Somalia, most of them not very pleasant to hear. Though epithets with which Amhara mothers curse the Somalis are truly fascinating, politics stand (at least slightly) above that.\nSomalia was subjugated over the course of the 16-17th centuries. The northern part was directly annexed and integrated, largely thanks to a channeling of the migrating Oromos into the formerly Somali lands, while in the south it was decided to set up a friendly Silcis Sultanate, a client state and a guarantor of peace. When the Imperial armies kept facing defeat after defeat in the north, the disloyal Somalis rose up in the south, with the Geledi clan coming out on top. In their barbarous ways, they wished to end Ethiopia and create an empire of their own. But our valiant armies have shown them that under no circumstance shall Ethiopia bow to the savages!

Kordofan was always the most unstable of the Empire's peripheries. None have dealt us as many problems as the Fur nomads, Dinka raiders and disloyal locals. The balance in the region was kept by an artificially created Oromo population, which was moved here by the Imperial authorities with a single goal - to wage war against everyone and everything. And as the Empire started to cruble, things went downhill pretty quickly, with the Fur completely overtaking the region by 1737. The barbarians terribly mismanaged the lands and commited horrible atrocities against the locals. However disloyal they were, it was our duty to restore order in Kordofan. And we have finally achieved just that.

The reconquest of Egypt was a heavy task. It was proposed countless times during the times of Marye of Yejju, it was his dream and an object of much thought and theoretisation over the years. But now, we have finally succeeded in reclaiming the Empire's crown jewel. Alexandria, the seat of the Coptic Patriarchy, has been reconquered, we control a large population of loyal Copts and untold resources granted by the fertile Nile - all of these things are, once and for all, ours. Or, well, the Emperor's. Depends on how you look at it. But in any case, such a move has certainly put Ethiopia into the spotlight of Mediterranean politics once again.

The days following the death of Marye of Yejju were full of political activity. The Enderase was a feared man, a brutish warrior who could kill a man with just his bare hands... during an audience in the Imperial Palace. The country's bureaucracy relied entirely on him, as he stuffed all important government offices with his loyalists. It wasn't much of a surprise when almost immediately all of them started bickering, with many commiting horrible crimes in an attempt to imitate Marye, only to end up imprisoned or straight up executed.\nThe Emperor didn't just sit in his palace. With his captors' attention tuned elsewhere, he gained the much desired freedom to scheme together with the many of his loyalists, of whom he, to his own surprise, found many among the servants of Marye's brutal regime. And yet he failed to throw off the shackles of the Regency - several men loyal to Marye and his 'cause' declared that the Regency will stay, but without a regent, with them ruling together as a group. Emperor Tewodros stood in firm oppostion to this. And, for the first time in his life, he was able to express his will, as the leader of one of the two rival political groups.

'Western ways are the future!' - tell us the traders.
'Their sciences have long since overtaken ours!' - tell us the educated men.
'Their vision of the Christ makes more sense!' - say the converted commoners.
Advancement often comes at a cost. Emperor Tewodros firmly believes that modernisation of Ethiopia is the future, for he his education was heavily influenced by men invited from the West. He saw the efficiency of the newer ways, he saw the decadence of Zemene Mesafint. But sometimes, new ideas bring dangerous things. What some of our people that have visited a western port even once say is oftentimes borderline treason, and and the Regency is taking full advantage of it. The Emperor is left with a choice: either punishing these men accordingly, or letting it go, which will have its own, far graver consequences.

The Negus Theodore, King of the kings of Ethiopia, had none of the insignia of sovereign majesty. Clothed very simply, he handled the pickaxe and the hammer like the lowest of his workmen, with the view of encouraging them by his example. He was in all things the man of energy, the fierce hero
- Emile Jonveaux, French traveller
Tewodros was nothing like what you would expect from an Emperor. Unless forced to, he rarely showed his royal descent, his high destiny or his the glory and majesty fit for the King of Kings. From early childhood, he mingled among the smallfolk, mastering the many arts and crafts of the commoners, and by that earning himself an impressive muscular physique.
But it is not the Emperor's duty to saw, plane and hammer, for there are countless men of lesser stature whose singular purpose from the state's point of view is to do just that. An Emperor must rule - that's his duty! And knowing Tewodros is a stubborn one, the Regency is taking full advantage of the Emperor's absence. Many are advising him to spend more time on combatting the Regency, for his commitment to a cause will bring massive results.

The Imperial bureaucracy is a heavy, clumsy machine that has degraded to relying purely on personal loyalties. Besides the fact that choosing a truly good and loyal clerk is an arduous and time-consuming task, there really isn't enough men out there to fill the roles. So, corruption inevitably surfaces: if your boss is paying you to cook the books, then you pay your subordinates to do the same!\nThis system creates a death loop, sort of a bubble, and when it pops, everything starts anew. Balance is eventually achieved, but at a heavy price. Perhaps, it would be wise to purge those for whom corruption became a habit, no matter the ruckus it will cause.

To most the news of the Negus' mental decline are just news, but recently more and more people have been feeling it on their own skin. Careless actions and weird, sometimes nonsensical orders have been an established status quo at the court for quite a while now. With time, the subordinates learned to create an imitation of obedience, pretending to follow the orders but never actually doing so. When such trickery falls through, Tewodros becomes furious, frequently executing the men he thinks are guilty, regardless of whether they actually are. Many are noting his resemblance with the old Marye of Yejju, who used to kill those who crossed him with his own bare hands.\nSuch terrible acts of violence are to be expected from Tewodros, say invited Western thinkers. All he knew from childhood was violence - he had seen it with his own eyes, he had to commit such acts himself in order to survive, and, with time, it became a habit. It's a miracle that this didn't begin earlier, they say.

They just never listen to me! I repeat time and time again, the garrison in Debre Markos is to be reduced down to 1241 men - for six months already! No, even more! Years! Decades! I told them to do it when I was twelve! Nevermind the regency, it wasn'teven that big of a thing for it. First Marye, then the idiots in Azezo, and now I have morons of my own! I should have replaced them already. And execute! Every single one of them! How could they mess up such an easy task?! It's thirty men less than I demanded! Goddamn saboteurs!

Today, Ethiopia and the whole Coptic world mourns, as news spread of Emperor Tewodros' death. To the surprise of many, he passed peacefully in his sleep - considering his habits in the recent years, it was more expected that he would walk out of a window in a fit of rage or get murdered in a plot. While his final years haven't been his best, he still is regarded as one of the best Emperors Ethiopia has ever had. His magnificent acts in both internal and foreign politics brought the country from a unrest-ridden backwater to a regional hegemon, with major reforms being implemented despite strong social stigmas. Tewodros' son, Prince Alemayehu, will now take the throne as Tewoflos I. He is not expected to be a political genius like his father, but with a good Western education and a sound mind, he is sure to keep the Empire in good shape.

Somalia is a divided land, one where all peoples are divided into clans - lineages predicated upon genealogical proximity to a shared ancestor. Layered in all aspects of life, the clan is both a tool for identification and a way of life. Clans define in practice the relationships between all people and actors in Somalia.\nThere exist five major clans: Isaaq, Darod, Dir, Hawiye and Rahanweyn (of which come the Geledi). All of them coexist within the Geledi Sultanate, a polity established in 1721 after the fall of the Silcis Sultanate, a puppet of Ethiopia. Though initially extensively participating in the traditional clan rivalry, in 1762 the Geledi supported the other Somali clans in a grand uprising against Ethiopian rule, which led to the complete independence of what is today Somalia and the creation of a shaky confederation, which exists to this day. But it is not a secret that this state of affairs is not to last, as an old enemy is once again showing its head: Ethiopia is recovering after years of civil war. If Somalia is to prosper, the clans will have to be put down.

Each of the five main Somali clans claims a certain territory, giving the Government a harder time managing and controlling it. Though destroying the ancient societal stigmas accompanying the clan structure is beyond our capabilities, weakening the political elites of those clans and enforcing egalitarianism in the higher echelons of power is entirely possible, and it will be a major step towards strengthening the State and solidifying our power.\n\n§BHover over each of the options to see the requirements to crush a clan.§!

The Somali Uprising of 1762 was a truly glorious show of Somali interclan cooperation, contrasting with the terrible performance of the Ethiopian forces during the events. The initial encounters with the local Oromos were hard-won, but the numbers eventually overcame the Oromo discipline and vigor, opening the way for the clans to advance north towards Harar. There, Somali tribesmen met the actual Ethiopian army in all of its glory (albeit heavily weakened by prior defeats) - and scored a major victory, massacring a major portion of the enemy army during their retreat.\nThe Battle of Harar was the last blow for the Ethiopian Empire, as tensions on the homefront became too much to manage and the Imperial Army had to retreat from Egypt and Nubia. But it was also the apogee for the Somali military campaign, as, following the battle, a large portion of the army was lost due to internal conflicts, starvation and disease in the prolonged siege of the fort of Harar. Further advancement into Ethiopia was impossible - the Somalis were stopped at the foothills of the Ethiopian Highlands. But the site of the great victory at Harar will not be forgotten anytime soon, for it is a living testament to Somali will and the power of cooperation.

With European encroachment into Africa imminent, we find ourselves in need of delineating our border. We will lay claim to the lands beyond the Rift Valley and draw a proper line there in order to not find ourselves in a border conflict with a much stronger power.

Maasai tribes have been defeated by our forces, and many of them are not willing to remain as subjects. As such, a large number of them started migrating west, towards the lake Ukerewe, displacing the local Bantu tribes.

We have done the unthinkable: the ancient Somali clan system, which has defined relations between people on all levels of life, has been defanged and destroyed on a governmental level. Our legislation now considers every Somali to be equal to his kin, and any discrimination based on clan affiliation is outlawed. Clans still exist in the minds of the people, but without the support base. In the future, we can expect the clans to fade entirely, and for the idea of a Somali nation to prevail among our people.

Maniyel was born to a common Christian family in the Nuba Mountains. His father wanted him to become a priest, just like himself, and the boy was educated accordingly - however, these plans were crushed, as the family was taken into slavery after a Fur raid on their village.

At the age of 19, Maniyel converted several dozen of his fellow slaves, most of whom were Dinka, to Christianity, and later staged an uprising against his captors. He and his band fled south, and, through wit and courage, he eventually became the most powerful chief of the region, having gathered an almost godlike reputation among the Dinka thanks to his impressive physique.

He assumed the title of Makk (King) and created a theocratic state, focusing the state's attention on spreading the Christian Faith, which was made easier by the semi-monotheistic nature of indigenous Dinka beliefs, as well as a similar Creation Myth.

After raising a strong army of Dinka tribesmen, he marched on Taqali and deposed the pagan authorities, seizing the state for himself.

He assumed the title of Makk (King) and created a theocratic state, focusing the state's attention on spreading the Christian Faith, which was made easier by the semi-monotheistic nature of indigenous Dinka beliefs, as well as a similar Creation Myth.

In $YEAR$, nearing the age of 60, Makk Maniyel has finally left our world. He died of a sudden illness contracted while preaching on the southern edges of the country, succumbing to it in just a few short days. It took a while for the news to reach Nubia, from where they spread to Ethiopia and Egypt, finally reaching the Partiarchate of Alexandria, with many voices immediately calling for his canonization. Meanwhile, in Maniyel's own congregation, things have been rather awkward, as the priests invited from abroad try to combat the myth of Maniyel's ascension to heaven, undoubtedly influenced by the population's recently pagan beliefs.\nNevertheless, the transition of power from Maniyel himself to his son was peaceful, and there is no doubt that Maniyel's conquests will continue.

Gondokoro Island, located on the east bank of the White Nile, is a trading station 1200 km south of Khartoum. Its importance lay in the fact that it was within a few kilometres of the limit of navigability of the Nile from Khartoum upstream. From this point the journey south to Uganda was continued overland. Due to this, it was a major hub of Christian missionary activity, beginning in the 17th century. Several missions have been set up here, including the most recent one in 1852 by an Austrian Catholic missionary Ignatius Knoblecher. None of them managed to survive due to the hostile environment, enemy raids, and other factors. Makk Maniyel decided to set up a massive administrative and military hub on the island, eventually moving his residence here, effectively making it the capital of the country.

The fabled Source of the Nile turned out to be a massive lake variously called Ukerewe, Nam Lolwe or Nyanza. The Europeans, however, thought that they could name it how they wanted to just because their explorers found it. Now we countrol the area around the lake, and we will name it how we want to.

The recent history of the Kurds is inexplicably tied to the Yazidi faith. Founded as an Islamic order in the 12th century, Yazidism combined secular and theocratic power in one man, a Shekh, who served the role of a political and religious leader. The faith became a force to be reckoned with in the 13th century, when the Greek assault on Anatolian Turks forced many of them to move east, with many of them passing through Yazidi lands and adopting the faith. The bolstered numbers of the Yazidi allowed Shekh Sharfadin to resist the Mongols and pass the rulership to his son Zeynedin, who, following the collapse of the Ilkhanate in the 1290s, expanded the domain under Ayyubid patronage. This is considered the founding point of the Sharfadin Shekhdom, also known as the Yazidi Empire.\nQuickly conquering large swathes of land, the Empire controlled most of Iraq, Eastern Anatolia and Western Persia, when an invasion by Timur brought the Yazidis to their knees, though remnants held out in Anatolia until 1435.\nAs of 1836, the center of Yazidi power lies around Lake Van, as Kurmanca proper was lost first to Ethiopia, then to a Greek-backed Assyria. And yet, maybe not all is lost for the Kurds.

Bedirxan is the hereditary head of the house of Rozhaki whose seat was the ancient Bitlis Castle. His dynasty ruled in Botan, the area currently controlled by the Assyrians, but during the Byzantine Expedition to Assyria in 1806 and the subsequent defeat of the Kurds, his family's domain was seized. He, together with the survivng members of his house, was forced to flee north, where he managed to overthrow the Emir of Bayazid and secure himself a new home. Bedirxan became known as a capable administrator, restoring the war-torn lands and allowing the population to grow massively. He also was a capable military leader, and in $YEAR$ he started his campaign against the neighboring Kurdish principalities to unite the independent Kurds and prepare to reclaim his domain down south.\nHis efforts were not accepted without resistance, as a Turkoman tribe under the leadership of Hizir Bey heard of the happenings as they were arriving from the lands west. Hizir decided to rally the resistance against Bedirxan, settling his tribe in Bitlis and becoming the de-facto Emir.

Our state is known by many names across the world. We call ourselves the Roman Empire, a name that has been passed down through millenia, our source of pride and a glorious legacy of the old Rome. But outside of the Empire's borders, names become not nearly as glorious, and oftentimes ugly and mocking. For the Russians and many Eastern Europeans we are known as the Greek Empire, a name despised by many as it is now thoroughly associated with the Hellenophiles. In Western and Central Europe, they use the name of our capital, the Byzantine Empire or the Empire of Constantinople.\nThere is no denial that to the outsiders, our claim to the legacy of Ancient Rome is doubtful at best, no matter how many reasons we might bring up to justify it. Times are changing, and modern diplomatic affairs require a single, centralised name for our country. It will be a hard thing to accept, but denial of the situation isn't going to help. Our mental reconciliation will have to start now.

When the Timurids swept away the Yazidi Empire, instead of chasing down the leftover tump states in Anatolia, they went into Syria and Egypt. The local Mamluks resisted with vigor, and yet, Egypt fell to Timurid forces in mere years. When their Empire collapsed in on itself due to succession crises, the Ethiopians swept in, quickly filling the power vacuum and reaching as far as Mesopotamia. Here, they transfered the administration of the conquered Yazidi lands to the local Assyrian Christians, who, despite having many religious disagreements with their Amhara overlords, were still viewed as more trustworthy than the Kurds. Persecution of the Yazidis was rampant, but despite multiple uprisings, the Ethiopians were only chased off in the 18th century. An Assyrian-Kurdish civil war ensued, which was barely won by Assyrian arms with the help of a massive Greek expedition.\nThe Assyrian power base is its Christian population, which only constitutes a plurality. Their weak state was unable to crush the Kurdish tribes, with many of them retaining a substantial degree of autonomy. They are undoubtedly disloyal - and a new Kurdish Uprising is already being prepared.

The defeat of Assyria completely changes the situation in the Middle East. The Christians have been pushed out of the region for the first time since the 16th century, and the self-proclaimed 'Protector of the Eastern Christians', a title taken by the Greek Emperor after their Assyrian Expedition, can't idly watch the Yazidis establish a strong state. Knowing that Constantinople will surely act up, we have sent them a delegation, asking to establish diplomatic ties in an attempt to mend the rift between us. And surprisingly, we weren't the only ones willing to come to a compromise - the Greeks realised that it was too late for an armed intervention, and they are now willing to come to terms with a Kurdish state on their border, but only if we concede some of our sovereignty. Our diplomats were able to secure this exact agreement: we give up all Arab-majority lands to neighboring powers, cease all attempts to incite the Anatolian Kurds to an uprising, and open our markets to the Greeks. The same diplomats tell us that these terms are final - if we decline, there will be war. What shall we do?

Assyria is a divided land. Kurds and Arabs, Nestorians and Miaphysites, Muslims and Yazidis - all of them live in the land between the Tigris and the Euphrates, brought here by the strange circumstances of history.\nThe Assyrians themselves were the underdogs of the Middle East since the Muslim conquest, through the Turkic-Mongol invasions, Yazidi rule and Timurid conquests. In the 16th century, Assyria was conquered by Ethiopia, who allowed the Christians to flourish for a price of spreading Coptic Christianity. Wars with the Sakarmans saw Assyria become a battlefield, and many of those discontented with Amhara rule fled to Shiraz, where Nestorianism was reinvigorated through the support of the Sakarman court, who sought to use it as a weapon. Indeed, in 1740 Ethiopia left Assyria, and it fell into Turki hands - then all Assyrians were united in the fight against the invaders, which was made easier with Greek support. Assyrians coalesced around the Patriarch of the East, who historically was the political leader of Assyria, and he became the ruler of a free Assyria when the Sakarman Empire fell into civil war in 1799.

In the final showdown, Assyria won. Whether by wit, superior armaments or tactics, or pure luck - we have crushed the Kurds, their largest uprising that we have ever met. No independent Kurdish state exists at this point, with their last mountain strongholds being taken by our armies. Now begins the long process of integration of the conquered tribes, who will need to be settled, educated and, maybe, converted to the True Faith.

Our efforts in integrating the Kurds have been largely successful, as expected. The nomadic pastoralist tribes are being encouraged to settle and participate in Assyria's economic system. Education in both Kurmanji and Assyrian has been implemented as well, which allows us to further streamline the dealings with the various tribes and slowly erase the familial identities. It seems like the Kurdish beast has finally been tamed.

The most horrible thing occurred: the Kurds and the Turks from the north have invaded our lands, their leader rallying the tribes in a daring attempt to claim independence for all Yazidis of our realm. Alongside the invasion from the north, several of the strongest Kurdish tribes rose up deep inside our lands, disrupting supply and ambushing our forces.\nSo begins the glorious fight for Assyria's survival - it isn't the first one, and it won't be the last one.

Our close ally in the east, Assyria, has found itself in an unfortunate situation. Having long experienced ethnoreligious tensions among its populace, Assyria was always ready to explode into a violent civil war between the Christian Assyrians and the Yazidi and Muslim Kurds and Turkomans. The burden that was too much to bear turned out to be the consolidation of the tribes around the lake Van by $FROMCOUNTRY$. With their support, an uprising occured in Assyria, supported by a full-scale invasion from the north.\nThis isn't the first time such a tragedy happened. Assyria practically owes its independence to us, as the newly-founded Assyrian state was almost destroyed in the late 18th century, when the region descended into infighting following the retreat of the Ethiopians. A military expedition sent by us in 1794 crushed the Kurds, albeit with heavy losses. It is due to the memory of this event, which is still very much alive in the hearts and minds of the polititians, we find ourselves unable to intervene again. We will do everything we can economically to support the Assyrians, but otherwise, we will have to hope that Assyria manages on its own.

As it becomes evident just now, neither hopes and prayers nor loans and arms were enough to secure Assyria's survival. They were utterly crushed by the Kurds, with many of their kind massacred by the heathens, with others fleeing towards Armeniakon. The Kurds promptly took over the former Assyrian lands, their forces reaching as far down south as Euphrates.\nSuch a failure of Imperial foreign policy caused substantial outrage in the capital. Once again, the Christians of the Middle East face a major defeat against the savages, with the Empire itself remaining as the only Christian power in the region. Although respected, such a rhethoric is very much less used than it would be expected, clearly indicating a change of times and a gradual movement towards more pragmatic and secular ways of reviewing foreign policy. A truly revolutionary change is the fact that the senate is willing to make a deal with the Kurds, as opposed to sending a direct military expedition. And it seems like the Kurds are willing to make compromises as well: we will recognize their state in exchange for them surrendering the Arab-populated lands and integrating their economy with ours.

The Assyrian population has traditionally been divided between different Christian denominations, with internal schisms worsening as time went on. The centuries of Ethiopian rule caused a fair bit of tension due to the spread of the Ethiopian version of Chrtisianity. Despite minor theological differences (of, at least, that is what they seem to us), this spread was done more often than not with unnecessary force. Attempts to root out the ancient Church of the East caused many of their adherents (Nestorians) to flee north, into the Kurdish lands in which the Ethiopian Empire had no power. Generally amicable relations between the Yazidis and the Nestorians have taken a steep turn for the worse as of recently, due to the now-independent Assyrian state moving towards religious acceptance of various Christian groups. Alleged misionary activities and ties to Nineveh have prompted us to attack, with our intention being to root out potential traitors and safeguard the flanks. Later estimates by Western scholars variously put the death toll from 10,000 to 15,000.

As the Kurdish and Turkish tribesmen were moving south, there wasn't a single man in their ranks who did not harbor a burning hatred for the Assyrians, born out of centuries of feuding. They were eager to satisfy their revanchist desires by any means possible.\nThough the authorities attempted to curb such sentiments, knowing that it would hurt out relations with the Westerners, nothing short of a disaster unfolded in Assyria. Many fled north, to Anatolia, or across the Euphrates. Others, however, met a most terrible fate...

Following the conquest of Van, Assyria found itself ruling over many more unhappy Kurds than ever. And it was not just the quantity, but the attitude of the locals that made the area truly a headache for the already stretched Assyrian bureaucracy to rule over. It was thus chosen that fast and decisive action was needed in order to quickly decapitate any rebellious sentiment the Kurds might have.\nAs Assyrian army regiments moved in to disarm the tribes, they quickly met heavy resistance from the locals. State of war quickly spread over the entirety of the newly-conquered area, with Assyrian soldiers often commiting atrocities against the civilian population. Despite these difficulties, without organized resistance the rebels soon surrendered one by one. Though the fallout of these events will linger in the air for quite a while, the overall action was a success, and only a small part of what will have to be done in order to cement Assyrian rule in the highlands.

In its long history, Egypt had seen many conquerors. The last of them, - or, perhaps, second to last, depending on who you ask, - was Ethiopia. With the help of the Greeks, they defeated the Mamluks in the 16th century and seized most of their domains in quick succession. It was a disaster for the Islamic world, as it was now split in two and faced the loss of key sites to the Christians. But Ethiopia proved to be a lesser threat than expected, as they got bogged down in wars with their Persian neighbors, which eventually led to their demise in the 18th century.\nAs Amhara armies were retreating, Egypt was left to fend for itself. The Copts attempted to organize a state of their own, which was met with heavy resistance from the Muslims, and the situation soon spiraled into an all-out civil war. Despite controlling key urban centers, the Christians did not have the forces to push out the Muslims, and soon an invasion by Muhsin ibn Alnas, a rebellious ruler of Muradid Cyrenaica, made the Bedouin cavalrymen place Alexandria under siege. This opened a prospect of Greek intervention - and so, a compromise was made: the Muhsinid dynasty would rule Egypt, but the Christian population would receive vast autonomy and privileges. A fragile peace was secured - but can the Muhsinids keep it?

Beirut, an important port city on the Phoenician coast, is the European gateway to the Middle East. Historically, it was a trade hub for merchants from all around the Mediterranean, who had extensive contacts with the local Christian population. The Muslim and Druze population is but a small minority compared to Christians - and all of these factors make Beirut a fully autonomous trade city, being able to sustain itself completely independently from the government in Cairo.\nTraditionally, the Greeks held the most influence in Beirut. Since the end of the Martletist Wars, however, Western European merchants started showing renewed interest in the region. Of them, the most active have been the Arelat, trying to fill the vacuum left by Italian merchants, who disappeared following the Egyptian Civil War. With them, they bring goods and wealth, helping the city's prosperity, but also missionaries and immigrants. News of potential opportunities attract those unhappy with their lives in Europe, most of whom are Jewish families, who have been moving to Beirut en masse. Beirut is thus Egyptian only in name - it is the first city to fall in Syriac hands.

Following the Greek invasion, disloyal elements in the Syriac society (of which it mostly consists) took heart all across Northern Sham. In areas occupied by the Greeks, they supported the invaders and joined their ranks, while in other places their protest took form of civil disobedience, or, in rarer cases, small-scale sabotage. The most egregious of such cases and a never before seen development is the formation of the 'Union for the Protection of Syria', a Syriac nationalist organisation with its proclaimed goal to create an independent Syriac state in all Christian-majority lands. While their reach is certainly limited and membership numbers relatively small, this highlights a new tendency among the Syriacs, though it should have been expected - Syriac Christians have not been accounted for in the Treaty of Alexandria, which established the infamous dichotomy of Christian-Muslim in Egyptian politics. We should expect to see the situation deteriorate.

Our concession to Greek demands was met with an immediate denouncement from Armenian circles in the country. Many Coptic priests, even those of Syriac ethnicity, called for their congregation to recall their support for Cairo. But, most importantly, disloyal elements in the Syriac society (of which it mostly consists) took heart all across Northern Sham. Calls for secession of Syria were made, though most of the time their protest took form of civil disobedience, or, in rarer cases, small-scale sabotage. The most egregious of such cases and a never before seen development is the formation of the 'Union for the Protection of Syria', a Syriac nationalist organisation with its proclaimed goal to create an independent Syriac state in all Christian-majority lands. While their reach is certainly limited and membership numbers relatively small, this highlights a new tendency among the Syriacs, though it should have been expected - Syriac Christians have not been accounted for in the Treaty of Alexandria, which established the infamous dichotomy of Christian-Muslim in Egyptian politics. We should expect to see the situation deteriorate.

Our pessimistic prognosis of the situation in Sham seems to be coming true. Increasing trade with Europe, increased amount of Jewish immigrants, the spread of western ideas and the feeling of impunity due to little action being done to counteract the disobedience makes the Syriac population more emboldened as time passes. The local economy has practically separated itself from the Egyptian, as more and more Christians refuse to pay taxes and instead opt for directing them to the Church, or, worse, to the Union (for Protection of Syria).\nBut this is just one side of the problem. Another massive issue that is arising just now is the resentment felt by the Muslim population. The most obvious reason is the fact that the Christians are left unpunished for tax evasion, which turns the ire of the Muslims both towards the Christians and the Government. Another reason is that as trade with Europe increases, merchants who are mostly Christians and Jews prosper, while Muslim residents face increasing economic hardships. This creates an extremely dangerous possibility of Muslim-on-Christian violence, which, if it were to happen, would surely have terrible diplomatic consequences in our relations with Constantinople and Europe as a whole.

The spark that was needed to kick off the violence has finally come on October 17th, 1850. Celebratory fire during the festivities led by Patriarch Maximos III Mazloum gave rise to rumours that Christians were arming themselves. On the evening of the same day, Aleppian residents protesting against the looming threat of conscription advanced to the predominantly Christian quarters of Aleppo, where they began to loot and pillage both churches and private homes. This took the Christians by surprise, but their already established practice of autonomy allowed them to soon mount the resistance against the Muslims and overpower them. By the next day, the city practically turned into a battleground. On October 19th, government forces have joined the fight, as the Christian militias almost completely took over the city and started a massacre of their own. Seeing as the Egyptian regiments began to fight alongside the Muslims, the Syriacs assumed that it was time for an all-out uprising. They proclaimed the 'State of Syria', but their calls never made it out of Aleppo, as the city was pacified on November 2nd. In the aftermath, thousands were left dead and the city was heavily damaged. Foreign powers will not turn a blind eye to these events...

We've been receiving reports of unrest in Egyptian Syria for quite a while now, but the last few days their amount has exploded tenfold. Out of the many dubious reports, we can make a clear conclusion: mass violence broke out in Aleppo. The Christians were attacked by the Muslims, which led to an uprising, which was violently suppressed by the Egyptian military, with casualties numbering in the thousands. An outrageous occurence, it requires a most forceful response, as we the Emperor still holds the title of the Protector of Eastern Christians. The hawks demand an immediate military intervention, while the cooler-minded individuals propose sending a demand of vast autonomy for the Syriac Christians, one which the Egyptians are unlikely to accept, but it will at least give us a valid reason to invade.

As expected, it wasn't too long until the reaction from Constantinople came. And it was more lenient than expected, as instead of declaring war outrught, they demand that we grant self-rule to the Syriacs. The new Syriac state would have full internal sovereignty, but no external. The Christian majority of the Majlis is arguing that the best course of action would be to comply with this demand, as Egypt has no chance of winning against the might of the entire Imperial Army. The Muslims say that in reality, the Christian camp is jubilant with the Greek demands, as accepting could potentially mean them gaining a supermajority in the Majlis, and, by extension, unlimited power. Though the vote in the Majlis will surely be won by the Christians, it would not be a supermajority, so the King could overrule their decision.\n\n§REmpowering the Christians in Syria will lead to their empowerement in Egypt. This choice is paramount to our political future.

The Union for Protection of Syria is a Syriac nationalist organisation formed in 1836 by Christians under Egyptian rule with the goal of obtaining full political independence as an independent Syriac state. Due to major shifts in the sociopolitical environment of Syria, the number of members has swelled massively in recent years, and the Union enjoys extensive support from virtually all Syriacs. It is no wonder that it would eventually spread outside of Egyptian Syria: Antioch, a city housing a large Syriac population, now serves as a hub where political activists of the Union can preach and organize freely. From Antioch, they smuggle goods and weapons, they plan operations and have recently started to interact with the authorities, voicing their desires to receive at least covert support in their efforts. So far the local government has been cautious when interacting with these groups, but no matter if we support them or don't, it is obvious that something bad is brewing in Syria.

Contrary to what we have expected, the Egyptians have accepted our demands, which means that there is now a large Syriac Christian autonomy under Egypt. We will see how the situation develops, but the Syriac populace sure is jubilant about this development.
Expectedly, Egypt has refused to grant autonomy to the Syriac. War it shall be!

The Wahhabi Emirate of Diriyah, which dominated the Arabian Peninsula for decades, has finally collapsed. It means that the Holy City of Mecca is left under the Sharif of Mecca, whose state is much weaker than that of the Saudis. We could demand his subservience, which would include land concessions. And if our help to the Hedjazi Uprising was enough, he will definitely be more enticed to accept our demand.

Our weakness following the defeat of Diriyah was sensed by our strongest neighbour, Egypt, whose envoy now demands the Sultan to become subservient to Cairo. It is obvious that we wouldn't be able to effectively defend ourselves in case of an Egyptian invasion. But we could always try.
The Sultan of Hedjaz has accepted our demand. He will now be subservient to us.

The crazed Sultan of Hedjaz, upon receiving the demand form our emissaries, immediately ordered them to be arrested and executed. This is a grave insult against Egypt: shall we launch an invasion to bring him to justice?

As days pass without a response from Egypt, it becomes evident that Egypt swallowed its pride and not only ignored the execution of their envoys, but also abandoned the plan to subjugate us. It seems like it was all a bluff all along.

Alexandria has traditionally been a major center of trade on the Mediterranean, maintaining its status since Antiquity. It served as a link between the East and the West, as many goods going to Western Europe were transferred through Alexandria at one point of another. The city's worth only increased following the Ethiopian conquest of Egypt, but soonafter its dominance was shaken by the discovery of an alternative route to India by the Arabs of Andalusia, who were forced to search for a replacement after Ethiopia massively raised tariffs for Muslim traders.\nThe decline of Ethiopia and of the Mediterranean trade in general made Alexandria lose much of its worth. A saving grace for the city was the rise in demand of cotton, but a long-term decline is inevitable and it doesn't seem like much can be done to reverse the global processes, which are the reason to Alexandria's malaise.

Alexandria's long decline has finally come to a close. The construction of the Suez Canal allowed much of the goods previously going through Egypt to be transferred directly by the sea, without making a stop in Alexandria. The Pearl of the Mediterranean has lost its value.

Imperial rule over Syria has been quite peaceful considering the unrest that plagued the region just a few decades ago. The reasons to this are obvious: a Christian government is viewed as more legitimate, since it supports its brethen politically, economically and socially, while never putting the heathens' inetrests above those of the Syriacs. But comfortable life conditions cannot fully suppress the political will of the nation: lack of an institutionalized autonomy bothers the most ambitious of the Syriacs, and they have recently started to cautiously consider the idea of an independent Syria (one under our protection, of course). The Patriarch of Antioch Ignatius Peter IV, leader of the Syriac Orthodox Church, recently pleaded the Emperor to grant Syria home rule, as a republic that would be legally bound to Constantinople. We could easily refuse and continue integrating the Syriacs into $COUNTRY_ADJ$ society, which could potentially yield greater benefits but it is unlikely that Syriac demands are going to simply disappear.

Our rule over Syria is strong, but the Syriacs are becoming more and more discontent since our refusal to grant them autonomy as a republic. They no longer view Constantinople as a saviour from Muslim oppression, and their opinions are slowly shifting towards considering us but another conqueror. But not all is lost: the Syriacs are still willing to cooperate, and their pleas have forced the government to take a turn their attention to the issue and take a careful look at what could be done to prevent Syriac outrage. One potential compromise could be the creation of an Exarchate, a semi-autonomous polity that would hand the local reins of power to the Syriacs while never legally separating Syria from $COUNTRY$. This time, however, refusal would have dire consequences: the tides of Syrian nationalism are on the rise, and it is unclear how long it takes until they completely lose faith in us.

Major Syrian towns are in flames, as a full revolt of the local Syriac population is ongoing. Greek and Muslim alike are being targeted in what could be concidered a civil war, with armed groups operating in the countyside and harassing our armies. The cause to all of this is the continued refusal to grant the Syriacs autonomy, which they have asked on terms that were very much not beneficial to them. Now, they fight for an independent Syria, completely free from our oversight.

Our allies in Constantinople have bested the armies of Egypt and taken the city of Deyr al-Zour, previously ruled by the local Bedouin tribes. Our border now neatly extends into their territory along the Euphrates. But considering the size of their recent conquest, maybe it would be better for them to hand over the city and the surrounding desert to us. Surely, they wouldn't say no to an ally?

On the western bank of the Euphrates lies the city of Deyr al-Zour, inhabited by Bedouins and a small amount of Christians. We gained control over the city following the liberation of Syria, but before we could fell comfortable ruling it, Assyria asked us if they could have it. They say that controlling the city would be more trouble for us than it's worth, considering the large swathes of the desert that the city overlooks. At the same time, granting it to Assyria would change nothing in terms of diplomacy, as the city would be owned by our close ally. However, Deyr al-Zour grants us a pathway to Iraq, which we would lose if we were to satisfy the Assyrians.
Constantinople has agreed to transfer us the city of Deyr al-Zour. We now control both banks of the Euphrates, at least in this exact point of the river.
The Greeks refused to give us free land. Boo-hoo, you greedy imperialists!

Ruling over the Arabian sands is, just like the sand itself, coarse, rough and irritating. It is easy to claim a lot of land, but very hard to back the claim with actual control, since there are very few permanent settlements deep in the desert. The issue could be insignificant enough to ignored, if not the possibility of another country laying claims on the very same desert: in this case, where would the border be?\nForced to contend with its loss in Syria, Egypt thought of this beforehand, and is now proposing to establish a proper border, at least on paper. Every party that has an interest in the Syrian desert would receive its own fair share of land with very straight borders, solving the issue for now. It doesn't mean that Egypt intends to surrender its claims on Syria, though.
Despite the aftertaste of the last war, the Greeks saw reason in our proposal to delineate the border. The Syrian desert is now fairly divided between all interested parties.

A decade has passed since the tragic loss of Northern Sham to the Syriacs, and the prospect of reclaiming these lands is becoming dimmer with each passing day. Our hopes that this situation would not last have found their expression in the fact that the administrative division has been left unchanged, with the big administrative region of Sham still covering the lands we don't control. The region also had a special order of governance, as the main positions in it were split between the Muslims and the Christians, with a set amount of posts dedicated to each group, based on the population. After the Syriac Crisis, the Christian seats have been left vacant, so the dismantlement of Sham and the establishment of smaller divisions would not have a direct effect. But it would definitely be a sign that the reclamation of Sham is becoming more of a distant dream than a current political goal.

The Middle East is an area of historical interest for $COUNTRY$. Lost during to an invasion by the Arabs in the 7th century, the area came to be Islamicized and largely assimilated by the Arabs, with small pockets of Christians holding on until Ethiopia restored Christian rule in the area. But despite cooperation with Ethiopia, the population of the Middle East still gravitated towards the Empire, seeing our customs as culturally closer.\nThe situation has not changed following the demise of the Ethiopian Empire. In 1818, following the signing of the Treaty of Alexandria, which created modern Egypt, the Senate bestowed the Emperor with the title 'Protector of the Eastern Christians'. Decades later, with $COUNTRY_ADJ$ troops firmly holding parts of the Middle East, these ideas have received a continuation in the proposals of Michael Meshaka, a Lebanese Greek and a historian who advocated for complete integration of the Christian Levant into the Empire. His ideas were immediately picked up by $COUNTRY_ADJ$ nationalists and were even supported by some influential figures in the Levant itself. Though their foundation is flimsy, the ideas of integrating the Levant may be an opportunity for $COUNTRY$ in the future.

Dayru z-Zawr is a unique city in the regard that it lies surrounded by endless desert. Nearest urban centers of comparable size are either on the opposite side of the Euphrates, or across the said desert, hundreds of kilometres away. And thanks to its location, Dayru z-Zawr was the single most important stronghold that allowed to control the Syrian Desert, with there being no other alternatives if one wanted to exert even a modicum of influence over the vast area. But the remoteness of the city also led to the logical result of it being taken over by the local Bedouin tribes upon the collapse of the Sakarman Empire. No neighboring power had both the desire and the strength to enforce their rule in the city, so the Egyptian King eventually established a form of vassalage with the locals.\nBut Dayru z-Zawr's isolation was not to last. Thanks to never methods of transportation, especially the steamer boats, the city is much more accessible now, and the banks of the Euphrates house more and more settlements and outposts, bringing civilization closer to Dayru z-Zawr and integrating it into the larger politics of the region.

The terrible events that happened in the years since Syria first stood up against us made us believe that the status of Syria as a battlefield was to remain firm for decades to come. But new developments prove that such certainty was completely unfounded. The Union for the Protection of Syria has reportedly been torn apart internally! Following the change in the political situation in Syria, a group within the Union declared the fight for Syria to be over now, and called for everyone to lay down arms - obviously, such an attitude was not met kindly among the hardline Syrian patriots, plunging the organization into a schism. And while the UPS is rapidly succumbing to infighting, the same changes in Syria made the common populace actually lay down their arms and go about their daily lives, finally being able to experience the peace that they gave up so long ago. Syria is thus, for now, pacified.

The autonomy of the Syriacs was perceived by all as a temporary measure, but in different ways. For the hardline Syrian Nationalists from the Union for Protection of Syria, it was but a stepping stone to total independence. But for the more level-headed, the original decision to grant autonomy was the beginning of something great: a foundation of peace in the Middle East. Egypt's parliamentary system allowed for long-term cooperation between thought-to-be-irreconcilable groups, and Christians now have a much greater share of seats in the Majlis, which means that the King's veto can be overruled by a majority consisting of Christians and Muslims swayed by us. The march of progress in Egypt proper is non-stopping, and the support for such ideas grow ever louder. Now, the Majlis of Egypt has formally asked us for negotiations on whether the Syriac Autonomy could rejoin Egypt fully. And we sure damn can...

Egypt's parliamentary system aws created with a vision of long-term cooperation between the Christians and the Muslims, whose differences were thought to be irreconcilable by many. But some did not understand the system at all, while others rejected it. But politics is politics, so the Reformist faction now has a big enough share of seats in the Majlis to overrule the King's veto, if acting in unison with the Reformist Muslims.\nThe next logical step towards dismantling the failed system that exists right now is to formally end the monarchy in a legal coup - but there is no such mechanism, unsurprisingly. Thankfully, our friends in Syria can give us the justification to carry out our plans - we asked them the question on what would be required for them to rejoin Egypt, and they say a Constitution and the supremacy of the Parliament, which implies that there will be no king. We will agree to that in private, as to not make our intentions too obvious, as the Conservatives were quick to denounce the answer... So, unless a mysterious force intervenes, the Levant has a great future ahead.

To the most esteemed Nerd in Cairo,

Kill yourself.

Worst wishes,
The Free Nation of Syria
Surprise-surprise! Egypt said yes! And we definitely didn't act out a scene that was pre-made. And Syria is deeefinitely not a sock puppet in this situation...

Due to reasons unknown, our Egyptian allies have suddenly changed their minds and decided to tear down the project that they have spent the better part of their political career on in what seems to be a sudden fit of schizophrenia. Though it is more likely that the King and his supporters somehow managed to infiltrate and destroy the whole scheme. But the reason is a thing that historians will figure out. What matters now is that we will have to fight for our independence.
unused

The Syriac Crisis of the 1850s led to the creation of a Syriac Autonomy within Egypt - a move that fit perfectly into the original ideals upon which the Egyptian Parliamentarism was built, but went completely against the reality of Egyptian politics and the path that the Egyptian government took. And it was through this idealistic move did those who believed in the principles agreed upon in the Treaty of Alexandria uproot the existing system and change it in accordance with those values.\nThrough clever political scheming, the Reformists cornered the Majlis into an ultimatum: Syria would only decide its fate in favor of reintegrating with Egypt if the primacy of the Parliament was enshrined in a written Constitution. The prospect of war, and even moreso of foreign intervention coerced even some conservatives into agreeing with Syria's demands. What followed was a legal coup: lacking the mechanism to legally abolish the monarchy, the Majlis placed the King's property under arrest on formal embezzlement charges, and then ordered to arrest the King. He, obviously, did not comply - and instead fled country after receiving no support from the army. Thus the Egyptian Monarchy met its end.

Not even the greatest challenges could break the will of the Egyptian people. Neither internal enemies in Syria, nor external in Constantinople have met their goal of dismantling our state. The Kings of Egypt bravely led us in these hard times, and received the favor of the people. The Majlis, the organ through which the voice of the people could be heard, was attempted to be made into a tool of foreign influence in our country. But it was not fooled, and did not succumb to outside meddling. Instead, with the adoption of final reforms that bring our country up to modern standards, the Majlis formally transfered absolute power to the King, who took up the traditional title of Sultan. Egypt thus shook off the last shakles imposed on it by the Treaty of Constantinople.

The Majlis is split. The Reformists, who have spent so long preparing a legal coup, have had their plans thwarted, and are now seeking alternatives. The King and his supporters prepare loyal forces to stop the Reformists' moves, if any happen. The atmosphere in Cairo is dense. There can only be one winner...

With the Syrian rebels starting an underground war against us, we are met with the sudden need to somehow smoke out the rats and make Syria a peaceful province like it once was. Having in mind the obvious advantages that the rebels have, our high command has come up with two solutions: either decapitate the Syriac organizations by killing their leadership in a police action, or provoke them for an open revolt and crush them with the help of the Army. The first option would be way less bloody but require extensive preparation, and the effects will only come after a few years. The second option would be quick, harsh but also very effective at destroying the rebels' resources.\nAnd if we are to avoid violence, there is a third option, a civilian one: simply grant them the autonomy they so desire. So, we have a difficult choice ahead...

The Melkites are the members of various Eastern Christian churchesthat have accepted the decisions of the Council of Chalcedon. The name comes from the Central Semitic root m-l-k 'royal', referring to the loyalty to the Byzantine emperor, but eventually became a denominational designation for certain Christian groups in the area. Its meaning slightly rolled back during the period of Ethiopian rule due to the Imperial loyalties of the Byzantine Rite Christians. The term has risen back into prominence in the 19th century due to the conflict over Syria, and now they are mentioned more and more often: loyalist groups have recently united into the Organization of Syrian Melkites, with their interests lying in representing the loyalist part of the population in Constantinople, and combatting the rebels that wish to see an independent Syria, most notably the Union for the Protection of Syria. They insist on institutionalization and wish to become Constantinople's foremost friends in the region.

Nights in Syria under martial law are quiet. The curfew requires all civilians to stay at home after 10 PM, though, frankly, there is no need for an average Syrian to stay up for that long - Aleppo isn't Paris, after all. And it is under cover of that quiet did the Greek agents begin their task. It was swift, it was brutal, and it was scarily efficient. The scope of the opaertion turned out to be even larger than initially expected - even low-level functionaries of the UPS were targeted. Syria would remember the day - or, rather, the night - when the First Syrian Resistance fell. Yes, the First.

Pan-Aramaic nationalism has been a hit recently. There is a growing number of those who wish to see the two banks of the Euphrates united, and while it is easy to brush them off as lunatics, maybe we should at least attempt to ask the Assyrian government on what they think, since they've got the same ideas growing at home?

Syria has relayed a crazy proposal to us - the unification of our two coutries into the united state of Beth Nahrain. It sounds weird, but... maybe it could work, as a federal entity, where we receive substantial autonomy... Wait, what's with tat tax collection business, where does it all go?..
Unexpectedly, Assyria said yes. We are now a single country!

Just as we thought, Assyria refused. The formal reason is that they're upset about the amount of autonomy of each member that this union would guarantee, to the point where what they suppose is just a close alliance. So, this idea dies right there.

Our colony of Ny Sjaelland has grown massively throughout the years, and it seems like a local political culture is beginning to form. Calls for home rule are heard more and more frequently, and perhaps we must give them some autonomy to better administer the territory.

The port of Nollaig, formerly owned by the Dutch East India Company and then called Stavenisse, was acquired for the Gaelic crown in 1831 following the Treaty of Calcutta, which heavily limited Dutch influence in the Indian Ocean. The port, though small and underdeveloped, turned out to be an extremely valuable asset in trade and a much needed resupply point on the way from India. The recent independence of the Cape could not have gone unnoticed by the colonial authorities, as small bands of Boers made their way to the Zulu Kingdom and attempted to settle in the area. Such a development may become a significant threat in the future, and it is at the very least conserninng as of now.

Continued Boer enroachment into the lands of the Zulu sparked conflict between the settlers and the natives. An unfortunate series of events led to several civilian Boers being killed by Zulu warriors, which forced several hundred well-armed Boers to begin massacring neighboring villages. The Zulu Kingd sent a large response force, outnumbering the Boers more than tenfold, and a battle ensued.\nThe colonial authorities in Nollaig were well aware of the happenings right outside of the city, and, deciding not to wait for an order from Dun Eideann, have devised a plan to stage a false-flag in order to weaken both sides. They sent a regiment of Black soldiers to flank the Boer cavalry, baiting the Boers to pursue them and, as such, attack Gaelic troops. When the deception became obvious, Gaelic troops were already in the process of practically occupying the entire area south of the Tugela River.

The Saudi court lies in shambles. News of defeat in the latest wars have caused a great upheaval across the country, leading to many of our subjects losing faith in the teachings of al-Wahhabi. Amidst the chaos, the ruling House of Saud has removed the major Wahhabi leaders from positions of power and taken over the government in its entirety. The Arab Slave Trade was a profitable business not just on the coast, but deep inland as well. Muscati outposts could be found deep inside of Africa, reaching all the way into the Congo basin. No effort to convert the locals was made, and instead the Arabs were ruthless and dealt with the natives without mercy. One of such slave traders was Tippu Tip, who has been centralizing his ivory and slave exploitation in Central Africa into an organized trading empire. He established the Sultanate of Utetera and brought thousands to Zanzibar.

The Arabian desert is hard to control, as the population of the region is only able to sustain itself in migration. But times are changing, and foreign powers to the north have established control over large swathes of this land, which they consider to be their territory now. Our claims to this part of the desert are now practically useless, as national borders force the locals to partake in the economic life of the region closest to them, driving the nomads away from us.
